stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO; Colette Kress steps in as interim chief
stories.why_read: Yesterday's edition flagged the board moving against him; now it has happened, and the company that sells the picks and shovels of the AI boom is without its founder for the first time since 1993.
body: Nvidia's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO, president and director on Thursday after an inquiry into his personal conduct, according to AP and posts summarized on X. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim chief while the board searches for a successor, and investor Harvey Jones is now board chair. Reports tie one of the relationships at issue to a woman alleged to have links to Chinese intelligence, and Reuters reports Huang also had a relationship with a second employee. Shares fell sharply on the news.

Inside the company the mood is mixed. WIRED reviewed an internal suggestion-box post urging the board to weigh employee sentiment that has drawn more than 1,600 comments, many asking for Huang's return. For anyone building on CUDA, the near-term question is less about the roadmap, which runs years ahead, than about who negotiates Nvidia's huge supply and financing commitments from here.

stories.headline: Google ships Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a fast agentic model that edges out its own frontier tier
stories.why_read: You retweeted Cursor's launch post: Hydrogen is already in Cursor, and Google pitches it as the fast executor that pairs with Carbon and Argon for the hard thinking.
body: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12 as its model for rapid execution across coding and agentic workflows, available across AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini app, Search, and Antigravity for paid tiers. Google says it scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level, ahead of Argon's 50, and 54 at its xhigh setting. Pricing is flat across the 1 million-token window: $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output.

Cursor says Hydrogen scores 54.3% on CursorBench at default effort, up from 39.6% for Gemini 3.8 Flash. In Antigravity, Google also added an Orchestrator option that moves work back and forth between Hydrogen and Carbon as a task evolves, rather than routing the whole job once from the first prompt.

stories.headline: Anthropic's IPO site goes live, with the listing confirmed for next Wednesday
stories.why_read: The prospectus numbers are now public, and you retweeted Theo calling them insane; this is the first frontier lab to open its books to public investors.
body: Anthropic posted its IPO roadshow site with a founders' letter, a roadshow video and Q3 2026 financial highlights, and its own post on X points investors to the S-1 on EDGAR. Theo of t3.gg reports the IPO is confirmed for Wednesday next week. Its Q3 highlights note that net loss includes a $21.9 billion non-cash charge tied to the change in fair value of convertible notes, derivatives and SAFEs as its valuation rose.

The roadshow leans on enterprise customers such as Bristol Myers Squibb, Accenture and AIG, and on a section about its approach to compute. Expect a week of analysts picking apart margins and compute spend, which will set the bar for how public markets price every other AI lab.

stories.headline: Bloomberg: SpaceX and Tesla in advanced merger talks for a roughly $3.4 trillion company
stories.why_read: If it happens, your two favorite Musk companies, from Robotaxi to Starship, end up under one ticker, with Terafab as the shared glue.
body: Bloomberg reports, per a summary of posts on X, that SpaceX and Tesla boards are finalizing terms after forming special committees last month, discussing price, governance and share swaps in an all-stock deal that could wrap up by December. The combined company would be valued around $3.4 trillion and span EVs, robotics, rockets, satellites and AI infrastructure.

The hurdles are real: regulatory and shareholder approvals, plus separating Tesla's China operations from SpaceX's U.S. defense contracts. Neither company has confirmed the talks, so treat this as reported, not done.

stories.headline: Starship Ship 42 rolls to the Starbase pad ahead of launch
stories.why_read: You retweeted the rollout photos: the next flight vehicle is on the pad, which usually means a launch window is weeks, not months, away.
body: SpaceX posted four photos of Ship 42 moving to the Starbase pad ahead of launch. The post does not give a date, so the next markers to watch are static fire and a license update.
For the why behind the flight profile, you also retweeted Farzad's short explainer, "Why Starship Circles Earth 14 Times Before Coming Home," which pairs well with the rollout.

stories.headline: Edge0 open-sources a 145B-parameter model that runs on a laptop
stories.why_read: Open weights plus the full inference stack, aimed squarely at frontier-class coding and agent work without a cloud bill.
body: Edge0 released Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B along with its unified inference framework and deployment tools, calling 145B the first open-source on-device model at that size. Its laptop comparison reports more than 80 tokens per second at 28GB peak memory. The earlier Edge0-35B phone model reportedly runs at 37+ tokens per second on an iPhone 18 Pro Max using about 2.5GB.

The team says it is shipping the full stack so others can reproduce results, fine-tune, and integrate the models. The claims are the vendor's own, so independent benchmarks on real laptops will matter more than the launch charts.

stories.headline: Forensics on published weights suggest Chinese labs trained on export-controlled Blackwell GPUs
stories.why_read: A clever technique: the evidence comes from the models' own weights, not leaks, and it lands in the same week as Nvidia's leadership crisis.
body: Unemployment Labs says six models released since April 2026 by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group carry numerical patterns that match Nvidia Blackwell hardware, while earlier models from the same companies match Hopper. The analysts recover traces of the models' initial values and search for hardware configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3 they confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips.

They are careful about the limits: the fingerprint shows how the weights were created and supports, but does not prove, that Blackwell also did the training. Specially configured AMD hardware is the only alternative they found, which they rule out for DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

stories.headline: Microsoft 365 outage knocks out Outlook and Teams for millions across dozens of countries
stories.why_read: Hours-long, global, and hitting banks, courts and the NHS: a good case study in what a single SaaS dependency can take down.
body: Microsoft said it is making additional progress toward recovery after an outage that left millions without Outlook email, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services. Downdetector said reports reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour, and Microsoft said the outage was not caused by a cybersecurity breach. The U.S. House said its engineers were working with Microsoft, and an NHS email disruption in the UK was expected to delay some prescriptions.

By Friday morning Eastern time Microsoft reported email delivery improving across a growing share of affected tenants. A separate Hacker News thread noted Outlook was still down after 12 hours, so expect a post-incident report worth reading.

stories.headline: WSJ: Nvidia's chip-financing guarantees ballooned to $530 billion before Huang's exit
stories.why_read: The quieter story under the scandal: Nvidia has been investor, lender, supplier and backup buyer to its own customers.
body: Per a summary of posts on X citing the Wall Street Journal, Nvidia's commitments to cash-strapped AI firms buying its chips reached $530 billion in the quarter ended July 26, including a $105 billion OpenAI-linked project. Interim CEO Colette Kress had reportedly questioned the deals and clashed with Huang over them.
Some initiatives are now reported paused. If that holds, the circular financing that helped fuel GPU demand could slow just as more customers build their own chips.

stories.headline: Nvidia employees petition the board to bring Jensen Huang back
stories.why_read: A rare inside look at how a founder-led company reacts when the founder is pushed out.
body: WIRED reviewed internal correspondence showing a suggestion-box post, written before Huang resigned, that asked the board to consider employee sentiment. It has since drawn more than 1,600 comments, many asking for his return, and one employee sent a companywide email demanding transparency about his exit.
Huang, 63, had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993. Nvidia and its new board chair, Harvey Jones, did not immediately respond to WIRED.

stories.headline: Rust 1.100 finally stabilizes the never type after ten years
stories.why_read: Five failed stabilization attempts later, `!` is real, and it cleans up a surprising amount of error-handling and match code.
body: The Rust team shipped 1.100.0, and the headline is the never type, spelled `!`, the canonical type for computations that never return a value, such as return, break and std::process::exit. Because a value of type `!` cannot exist, Rust allows it to coerce to any other type, which makes diverging branches in match and if expressions type-check cleanly.
The post notes this took 10 years and five failed stabilization attempts, and it completes a project goal. Update with rustup update stable.

stories.headline: A 22-year-old PostgreSQL type-confusion bug becomes a reliable RCE (CVE-2026-6460)
stories.why_read: If you run managed Postgres, read this: a new class of core bugs, found with an AI agent as tutor.
body: Mehmet Ince describes giving PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changing the type of one of its fields, and asking it to read the value back; the resulting type confusion led to what he calls one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploits he has seen. It is part 3 of his series on systemic risks in the managed PostgreSQL industry.

He started by exploiting pg_clickhouse and used an AI agent to work through Postgres internals one question at a time before the pieces connected. Check your provider's patch status for CVE-2026-6460.

stories.headline: SGLang hits v1.0 and launches an industry consortium backed by Nvidia, AMD and Google
stories.why_read: Open-source inference serving just got a governance home, with both big GPU vendors at the table.
body: At the first SGLang Summit in San Francisco on November 12, the project announced v1.0 with zero-overhead scheduling, Rust rewrites and support for 217 models used across 330 organizations, according to a summary of posts on X. LMSYS Org also launched the SGLang Consortium with NVIDIA, AMD, Google, Meta, Intel, Cloudflare, Modal and RadixArk.
Banghua Zhu also presented Miles v0.2. The summit runs through November 13.

stories.headline: Matt Pocock's "Home Repo" pattern for agents that span many repos
stories.why_read: You retweeted this: a simple answer to where skills, steering files and tooling live when your agent work crosses repositories.
body: Matt Pocock says working with agents across multiple repos is a pain because there is no obvious home for skills, steering files and tooling. His answer, which he has used for months and almost thought too obvious to post, is a dedicated Home Repo, explained in a nine-minute video.
It maps well to a fleet-of-bots setup: one place for shared conventions, with each working repo staying lean.

stories.headline: Your Claude Code setup may be tuned for a model you no longer use
stories.why_read: You retweeted this AIE CODE talk: what to cut from CLAUDE.md, what permissions should enforce, and where tests and CI should take over.
body: Anthropic's Lydia Hallie argues at AIE CODE that many agent setups carry instructions written for older, weaker models. Her talk covers what to trim from CLAUDE.md, what permissions should enforce instead of prose, and where tests and CI should do the checking.
The general lesson holds for any agent harness: re-audit steering files whenever you change models.

stories.headline: GitHub: 1.2 billion commits in one week, and reviews are the new bottleneck
stories.why_read: You retweeted GitHub's guide; the numbers explain why plan, verify and observe matter more than generation now.
body: GitHub's Nick Liffen and Philip Holleran write that in October GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week, more than in all of 2025. They cite a Faros AI study finding pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams moved from low to high AI adoption.

The guide walks through Plan, Build, Verify and Observe with Copilot features such as stacked pull requests, Agent Merge, AI Scan, Copilot Dreaming for memory upkeep, and Copilot Fusion for picking models and reasoning depth.

stories.headline: Grok Bot on Mac can now use Messages, Mail, Notes, Reminders, Calendar, Location and Contacts
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this: your bots can now reach the Mac's built-in apps directly.
body: The Grok Bot account announced that Grok Bot on Mac now works with Messages, Mail, Notes, Reminders, Calendar, Location and Contacts.
Separately, a post you retweeted from Alex says Grok Bot is quietly getting better at browsing the web without tripping bot detection, thanks to many behind-the-scenes changes.

stories.headline: The Cybercab math: a million cars a year needs about 20,000 dedicated charging stalls
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this thread: a first-principles look at whether Tesla's Cybercab ramp and its charging build-out add up.
body: Genma_Jp argues Tesla's stated 125,000-unit Cybercab capacity is conservative: a Model Y line at roughly 30-second takt time gives about 1 million vehicles a year, and Tesla's Cybercab target is 10 seconds. Ending Cybertruck around mid-2027 for more Cybercab lines points the same way.

The catch: if Tesla owns most of the fleet and one Supercharger stall supports about 50 Cybercabs, 1 million cars need about 20,000 dedicated stalls, versus roughly 6,000 U.S. stalls added per year today. Either big charging hubs start by early 2027 or the line runs slower. Those are the author's estimates, not Tesla's.

stories.headline: SpaceX orders a 100 GW-a-year solar cell line for orbital data centers
stories.why_read: Energy tech meets space: SpaceX is going vertical on heterojunction solar to power its Starmind compute satellites.
body: Per a summary of posts on X, SpaceX signed with Germany's Singulus Technologies for a turnkey line able to make 100 gigawatts of heterojunction solar cells per year, with first delivery planned for early 2027 at its Bastrop, Texas satellite factory.
The cells are for Starmind satellites, orbital AI data centers with large solar wings and Nvidia hardware in sun-synchronous orbits. Musk called it the start of the project.

stories.headline: The first GraphQL over HTTP spec is out
stories.why_read: You retweeted this: an official spec for how GraphQL travels over HTTP, which should end years of per-server quirks.
body: The GraphQL Foundation announced the first released version of the GraphQL over HTTP specification.
For architects, it gives client, gateway and server vendors one shared reference to conform to, which simplifies interoperability testing across stacks.

stories.headline: Jane Street is changing its software engineering interviews for the agent era
stories.why_read: When code is cheap, taste and verification matter more; here is how one demanding employer is testing for that.
body: Jane Street says most of its engineers now use LLMs daily for writing, reading, debugging and reviewing code, but its interviews had not changed. This summer it began trialing new onsite interviews for campus candidates that involve less code-writing and more software design and verification of the quality, structure and intent of code.
The firm says the goals stay the same: see how candidates solve problems, structure work, communicate and collaborate.

stories.headline: Brave Search API now takes per-request agent payments over x402
stories.why_read: No API keys or plans: an agent with a USDC wallet can pay for each search on the spot, an early working example of agentic payments.
body: Brave added support for the open x402 payment protocol to its Search API. A request without payment gets an HTTP 402 Payment Required response with the price; the agent signs a USDC payment and retries, and Brave runs its own facilitator on the Base network.
Brave says other networks and stablecoins are coming. It covers both LLM Context grounding and general web search.

stories.headline: Apple's Foundation Models framework now works with any LLM
stories.why_read: A native Swift API that spans on-device models, Private Cloud Compute and third-party LLMs could become the default way iOS apps add AI.
body: Apple describes the Foundation Models framework as a native Swift API for integrating any large language model into an app, including direct access to Apple's on-device and Private Cloud Compute models. Built-in features include guided generation, tool calling, image understanding and Dynamic Profiles.
Multimodal prompts let apps pass images with text, and the Vision framework adds on-device OCR and barcode tools the model can call.

stories.headline: Europe's EV sales jump 49% as global sales rise 8% in October
stories.why_read: A data check on the EV transition: Germany's EV share topped 45% of new car sales.
body: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence data reported by Electrek show 2.09 million EVs sold worldwide in October, up 8%, bringing the year to 17.5 million. Europe sold 510,000 EVs, with battery-electric sales up 49% and plug-in hybrids up 7%.
Germany's EV share topped 45% of new car sales, and North America posted its first year-over-year increase of 2026, though Electrek says that rebound comes with a catch.

stories.headline: Rubin Observatory finds a likely dwarf planet on a tilted orbit beyond Pluto
stories.why_read: Early proof of what the Vera Rubin survey can do: a large new object in the outer solar system.
body: Smithsonian astrophysicist Matthew Holman and colleague Kevin Napier, sifting Vera C. Rubin Observatory data with a custom program, spotted 2026 ED138, a dwarf planet candidate whose orbit is tilted nearly 25 degrees relative to the main planets, a hint that Neptune disturbed it. The Hacker News post puts its orbit at roughly 280 years.
They had already flagged more than 2,000 new small distant objects, and they confirmed this one in archival images from the past decade.

stories.headline: A dead star spinning every eight minutes is sending radio pulses from orbit around a Sun-like star
stories.why_read: A first for long-period radio transients, and clean enough data to see which star is doing the pulsing.
body: Curtin University researchers at ICRAR linked radio pulses to GPM J071507-114153, a white dwarf that spins every eight minutes paired with a G-type star like the Sun. It is the first time such pulses have been seen from a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star rather than a cooler red dwarf.

Around a dozen long-period transients have been found since 2021. Lead author Sam McSweeney says the pulses are clear enough to track the white dwarf's orbit, placing the source at or near the white dwarf.

stories.headline: Euclid's first major data release maps 900 million galaxies
stories.why_read: 1.7 petabytes of free data aimed at dark matter and dark energy, and only 14% of the planned survey.
body: Per a summary of posts on X, ESA's Euclid DR1-Foundation dataset covers 1,900 square degrees from 13 months of observation, including galaxy cluster Abell 3128 and about 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates, the largest such catalog yet.
The release is free via ESA's Euclid Data Space, with deeper analysis expected in 2027.

stories.headline: Lake Travis is 101% full
stories.why_read: You retweeted this one: a happy hometown headline after years of drought worries.
body: Austin meteorologist Tommy House posted an evening photo of Lake Travis at 101% full.
It is a welcome sight for Central Texas water supply, and a good excuse for a weekend drive to the lake.

stories.headline: smolmaxxing runs the biggest LLM it can on TV boxes, a 2013 iPad and old phones
stories.why_read: Hacker energy at its best: custom kernels and flash-streamed weights to get real tokens out of e-waste.
body: The smolmaxxing project finds the largest model idle hardware can really run, then pushes further with custom kernels, careful memory use and weights streamed from flash. Every number is measured on the device.
Examples include a Xiaomi TV Box S with about 1GB of usable RAM running Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tokens per second, plus a jailbroken 2013 iPad Air and a OnePlus Nord CE 2.

stories.headline: OpenAI and Anthropic out-earn China's top six AI firms nearly 10 to 1
stories.why_read: Context for the IPO week: Epoch AI estimates put U.S. lab revenue in a different league.
body: Per a summary of posts on X citing Epoch AI estimates, OpenAI and Anthropic reached a combined $105 billion annualized revenue run rate by late September, versus $11 billion for six top Chinese firms. ByteDance led China at $4 billion, and DeepSeek hit $1 billion after doubling in September.
Quarter over quarter, Anthropic grew 47% and OpenAI 50%, while Chinese labs compete on low prices and open weights.
